questions.title: Can fair use be decided at the 12(b)(6) pleading stage before any discovery?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about how the court could dismiss Santos's copyright claims based on fair use at the motion to dismiss stage. I thought fair use was a fact-intensive inquiry that usually requires developing a factual record. The court cites TCA Television Corp. for the proposition that fair use "may be so clearly established by a complaint as to support dismissal." But how can a court determine transformative use, bad faith, or market harm without discovery? Is this unusual, or can fair use always be decided on the pleadings if the facts are clear enough?

questions.title: Why does the 'reasonable observer' standard control the transformative use analysis instead of the creator's intent?
questions.question_body: The court rejects Santos's argument that his videos were created for the same purpose that Kimmel used them for (commentary on Santos saying absurd things for money). The court says that whether a use is transformative 'turns on what a reasonable observer thinks, not the subjective intent of the copyright holder.' But Santos claims he was 'instigating' the creation of the videos through his Cameo requests. If Kimmel effectively designed the purpose of the original works through his fake requests, why doesn't that matter? What exactly is the 'reasonable observer' looking at - the works themselves, or the context of their creation?

questions.title: Does bad faith or misrepresentation negate fair use after Harper & Row?
questions.question_body: Santos argued that Kimmel's use of fake names to solicit the Cameo videos constituted bad faith that should nullify the fair use defense, citing Harper & Row's statement that 'fair use presupposes good faith and fair dealing.' But the court says the Supreme Court has 'since distanced itself from this statement.' I'm confused - what is the current status of bad faith in the fair use analysis? Can deliberate deception in obtaining copyrighted material ever preclude a fair use defense, or is the analysis now purely about the four statutory factors?

questions.title: What distinguishes market 'usurpation' from market 'devaluation' under the fourth fair use factor?
questions.question_body: The court says Santos suffered no market harm because the fourth factor asks 'not whether the second work would damage the market for the first (by, for example, devaluing it through parody or criticism), but whether it usurps the market for the first by offering a competing substitute.' This distinction confuses me. If Kimmel's use made Santos's Cameo videos less valuable by mocking them, isn't that market harm? What exactly makes something a 'competing substitute' versus merely critical commentary that might incidentally harm the market?

questions.title: Why didn't Santos have standing as a third-party beneficiary to enforce Cameo's Terms of Service?
questions.question_body: The court dismisses Santos's breach of contract claim because he wasn't a party to the Terms of Service between users (like Kimmel) and Cameo. The court notes there's a 'strong presumption against conferring benefits to noncontracting third parties' under Illinois law, and that other provisions of the Terms did contain third-party beneficiary language. But Santos is clearly the 'talent' on Cameo and seems to be the intended beneficiary of user obligations. What exactly does a plaintiff need to show to overcome the presumption against third-party beneficiary status? Would explicit language always be required?

questions.title: What must a plaintiff plead to establish an implied-in-fact contract under New York law?
questions.question_body: The court rejects Santos's claim for breach of implied contract because he failed to 'allege, in nonconclusory language, . . . the essential terms of the parties' . . . contract' and didn't plausibly allege 'an indication of a meeting of the minds.' I'm struggling to understand what would have been sufficient here. Santos and Kimmel did have interactions through Cameo - doesn't that imply some kind of agreement? What are the 'essential terms' that need to be pleaded for an implied contract claim, and how specific do those allegations need to be?

questions.title: Why does New York's fraudulent inducement claim require 'out-of-pocket' loss rather than benefit-of-the-bargain damages?
questions.question_body: The court dismisses Santos's fraudulent inducement claim because he 'failed to allege that he suffered any actual out-of-pocket loss.' But Santos did provide services (the Cameo videos) that he wouldn't have provided but for Kimmel's alleged fraud. Isn't that a loss? What exactly is the difference between 'out-of-pocket loss' and 'benefit-of-the-bargain' damages in New York fraud law, and why does fraudulent inducement specifically require the former?
